No score was inflated to compensate for this; see justification.
justification: PRIMARY VALUE-ADD IS REAL AND DIFFERENTIATED. Use The Index Luke's concatenated-index page teaches column order through a hypothetical employee/subsidiary merger and a telephone-directory analogy, backed by EXPLAIN plans pasted from five different engines with no timing; its B-tree page uses an abstract 4-entries-per-node illustration with a made-up log4(N) formula and no real database. This article instead generates one real 300,000-row SQLite table, reads the engine's own dbstat virtual table for the actual page counts (root 1 page/5 keys, 6 interior pages up to 442 cells, 2,518 leaves), and turns those real numbers into a 'prove the depth barely grows' exercise -- a genuinely different, more concrete angle than either the abstract-diagram treatments the brief worried about or Use The Index Luke's own hypothetical-schema approach. The composite-index section uses its own visitor_id/hit_at web-log data and a two-way-sorted figure, not Use The Index Luke's directory analogy or employee/subsidiary table. No overlapping running example, dataset, or distinctive phrasing found between the two. FABRICATION CHECK: I independently fetched all seven cited SQLite/Microsoft pages (queryplanner.html and optoverview.html twice, once via raw HTML grep, to be sure) and checked every quoted fragment word for word. All of the following are accurate, verbatim, and correctly attributed: the four EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN fields (eqp.html), the SCAN/'full-table scan' and SEARCH/'only a subset of the table rows are visited' definitions (eqp.html), 'the entire content of the table must be read and examined...' and 'still much faster than doing a full table scan' and the fruit/state 'simply ignoring the state column' example and the 'never contain two indices where one index is a prefix of the other' rule (all queryplanner.html), the interior/leaf page and K-keys/K+1-pointers structure and the left/right pointer-ordering rule and 'one index b-tree...for each index in the schema' (fileformat2.html), the covering-index mechanism and 'saves one binary search for each row' (optoverview.html), the LIKE-optimization BINARY/NOCASE pairing -- this one I verified against the raw HTML because a summarized fetch first returned a paraphrase; the article's quote is in fact a verbatim match to the page's bulleted list ('For the LIKE operator, if case_sensitive_like mode is enabled then...'), just trimmed of its opening four words, so no misquote -- 'the query planner does not do algebra' (expridx.html), and 'a lightweight ADO.NET provider for SQLite' (Microsoft Learn). I found no misattribution surviving in the final text; whatever two errors the writer says they self-caught, none of the checkable quotes and paraphrases in the current draft misrepresent their cited page. FILLER/AD CODE: none. First sentence states a concrete result, not a generic opener; no restated title, no 'in this article', no summary-of-headings conclusion (the closing section synthesizes a decision rule instead); no ad, consent or analytics code anywhere. TOOLCHAIN PLACEMENT: correct. The opening paragraph is pure content; the SQLite-3.50/one-session note sits at the end of the first SQL block's discussion (needed for reproducibility, not a provenance stamp); the full toolchain sentence ('.NET 10.0.12 on Windows 11, an 8-core x64 desktop (Intel Core i7-11700K)') appears exactly beside the first real C# timing measurement, as the brief requires. The 3.50-vs-3.41.2 SQLite-version mix is disclosed honestly and locally ('which need not match the 3.50 running the blocks above'), not glossed over. STRUCTURE VARIETY: confirmed distinct from both siblings. All three databases articles avoid boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion' headings, but relational-model-and-keys ends on a full ER diagram plus a 'what declarations cannot say' constraints-cost discussion, sql-joins ends on the three join-algorithm complexities, and indexes ends on a synthesized 'when does an index earn its keep' decision framework -- three different closing moves, not a shared template. Exercises are embedded mid-article in all three, but indexes' three exercises are 'Prove the depth barely grows' (prove-it), 'Predict the plan' (predict-the-output, but over EXPLAIN plans rather than program output, matching neither sibling's first-exercise form), and 'Make the index earn its keep' (fix-the-query/extend-the-code). No output is shown above any :::solution::: block in any of the three. RATIO CLAIM: 'roughly two thousand to five thousand times faster' is arithmetically consistent with the stated ranges (7.6-7.8 ms / 0.0014-0.0037 ms = ~2,054-5,571x) and is explicitly hedged as noise-dominated ('once a measurement drops to a few microseconds it is mostly clock resolution and cache state, not signal... treat the exact multiple as noise and the order of magnitude...as the finding'), not presented as a precise universal constant. run-code.mjs confirms PASS, blocks=40, executed=20, matching the writer's claim exactly. WHY NOT >=8.5: one real, unhedged navigation problem. The body contains zero internal links -- not even to the two already-published prerequisite articles this one is built on (relational-model-and-keys, sql-joins) or to the existing /glossary/#index-database entry that sibling articles already link to for the same term -- and there is no docs/crosslinks/databases/indexes.md recording planned links, so the brief's exemption for missing sibling links does not apply. This is the same class of finding that held sql-joins' round 1 below 8.5 (there, one thin glossary link plus a missing crosslinks file; here, no in-body links at all). Second, smaller finding: of the 7 sources in front matter, lang_createindex.html (CREATE INDEX syntax reference) is never cited or alluded to anywhere in the body -- every `CREATE INDEX` statement on the page is used without attribution to its own syntax reference, even though the other 6 sources are all cited multiple times. Both are quick, mechanical fixes; the writing and verification underneath them is strong.
